transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

I’m here because something at work has been getting really hard to manage. I teach preschool, and whenever I see balloons at school—even if they’re just down the hallway and not actually near me—my body reacts before I can even think. My chest tightens right away, and I kind of freeze for a moment, like my brain stops and I can’t immediately focus on what I’m supposed to be doing with the kids or in the classroom.

It sounds silly when I say it out loud, because they’re just balloons, but it happens so fast. I’ll spot one across the hall, and for that moment I’m just stuck, trying to get myself back together.
How long have you had this reaction to balloons, and does it happen every time you see them?

It’s been about seven months now. I can pretty much trace it back to one specific day at school, actually—a children’s art celebration we were having, and there were balloons around for decoration. One of them burst really close to my face, like right near me, and it startled me so badly.

Since then, that reaction has been happening when I see balloons. It’s not something I remember having before that, at least not like this. I keep thinking it should have worn off by now because it was just one balloon popping, but it’s been months, and it’s still there.
When you see balloons now, do you notice any other physical sensations or feelings of anxiety besides your chest tightening and freezing up?

Mostly it’s that immediate jolt of anxiety, like my body reacts before I’ve really processed it. The second I spot a balloon, even if it’s all the way across the hallway and not close to me, my chest tightens and I sort of freeze. It’s like for a moment I can’t think clearly about what I’m supposed to be doing—like where the kids are, what activity I’m leading, what I was about to say.

It’s not even that I’m standing there deciding to be scared. It’s just this automatic fear response, and then I have to work to pull myself back into the classroom situation. That moment of freezing is probably the part that bothers me most, because at work I need to be present and able to respond quickly.
Do you find yourself avoiding certain places or events at work where you might see balloons?

Yes, I do. More than I’d like to admit, honestly. At school, birthdays are the biggest one, because sometimes families bring balloons or the classroom has them for decorations, and lately I’ve been asking my aides to handle the birthday circle if I know there are balloons involved. I’ll make it sound practical, like, “Can you lead this part while I set something up?” but really it’s because I don’t want to be standing right there near them.

And with festivals or school events, if there’s a table with balloons tied to it or a balloon arch or anything like that, I tend to move away from that area. I’ll find some reason to be on the other side of the room or help at a different station. If I absolutely have to stay nearby, I keep as much distance as I can and try not to look directly at them. I kind of focus on just getting through whatever I’m supposed to be doing until I can leave that spot.
Outside of work, if you see balloons in other places—like at a store, in someone’s yard, or at a public event—do you still have that same anxious reaction, or does it only happen at school?

It’s definitely strongest at school. That’s really what brings me in, because when I spot balloons there—even if they’re just down the hallway and not right next to me—my chest tightens immediately and I freeze for a second. It’s like my brain kind of blanks before I can get back to thinking clearly about what I’m supposed to be doing.

At school that feels especially scary because I’m responsible for the kids, so even that brief moment where I’m frozen and trying to reorient myself feels like too much. I’m not saying I love seeing balloons anywhere else, but the reaction I’m most aware of and most worried about is when it happens at school, because I need to stay focused and functional there.
Has this reaction to balloons caused you any significant distress or affected your ability to do your job or engage in activities outside of work?

Yes, it has. I wish I could say it was just uncomfortable and I could push through it, but it’s started to actually affect how I do my job.

Like with classroom celebrations, especially birthdays, those are normal parts of preschool. They’re supposed to be sweet and simple, and I’m usually the one leading the circle or helping the kids sing or managing the little routine around it. But if there are balloons, I’ve been handing that off to my aides more often. I’ll say I need to get something ready or check on something, but honestly, it’s because I don’t want to be up there next to the balloons and then freeze in front of the kids.

And there was a festival art table I had planned to help with, and I ended up not helping because there were balloons nearby. That felt worse because I had actually been involved in planning it, and then I kind of backed away from it when it was time. My supervisor noticed, too, which was embarrassing. I don’t think I got in serious trouble or anything, but just knowing she noticed made me feel like this isn’t just in my head or just a small annoyance anymore. It’s interfering with things I’m supposed to be able to do at work.
Have you noticed any similar reactions to other objects or situations that remind you of the balloon popping incident, even if they aren’t balloons?

I don’t think so… at least nothing that stands out to me the way balloons do.

I’ve tried to think about that, because part of me wondered if maybe it was the popping sound in general or party decorations or something like that, but I haven’t really noticed the same kind of reaction with other things. Like, if I see streamers or signs or party plates, that doesn’t bother me. It’s really the balloons themselves that catch my attention and make me feel like I need to get away from them.

I guess I’m not completely sure what would count as “reminding me” of it, but I haven’t had that same freeze-up with other objects, no. It seems pretty specific to balloons.
If you see a balloon in a completely safe setting, like a balloon that’s tied up and not moving, or a picture of a balloon, does your body still react the same way as it does at school?

It’s not exactly the same in every setting, I think. A picture of a balloon doesn’t usually do to me what the real thing does, at least not in that full-body way.

But if I’m at school and I spot an actual balloon, even if it’s tied up and even if it’s not right near me—like if it’s just across the hallway—my body reacts before I can really talk myself through it. My chest tightens right away, and I kind of freeze for a moment. It’s not like I’m making a decision to be scared; it’s more that I see it and there’s this pause where I can’t think clearly about what I’m supposed to be doing next.

That’s the part that worries me most, honestly. At school, even a balloon that looks harmless still makes me react immediately, because I’m suddenly focused on it instead of on the kids or whatever task I was doing. A picture is easier to dismiss, but an actual balloon in the school setting can still set that off pretty quickly.

When you see a balloon at school and your chest tightens, do you ever feel like you need to leave the situation immediately, or do you mostly just try to manage the reaction while staying where you are?

Usually I try to stay if I can, but… lately I have been avoiding it more than I’d like to admit.

If it’s something like a birthday circle and there are balloons nearby, I’ll ask one of my aides to lead it or take over that part. I’ll make it sound practical, like, “Can you start the song while I grab something?” but really I’m trying to get myself away from the balloons before I get stuck just staring at them or feeling like I can’t function normally.

And with bigger things, like festival tables or activities, if there are balloons close by, I’ll move away or find some other job to do. I don’t always literally run out, but I definitely create distance. If I absolutely have to stay in the room, I try to keep myself as far from them as possible and just focus on getting through the moment without looking at them. Like I’ll keep my eyes on the kids, or on the supplies, or on whatever task is right in front of me, because if I look at the balloons too much, I feel like the reaction gets worse.
